ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. Uploaded PDF, 52 pages, image-only (Limon-font-era scan, read via page rasterization).
text:
Common on-farm corn storage methods in Cambodia include sacks and small home warehouses/stores; storing corn still on the cob (unshelled) generally keeps better and longer than storing shelled kernels, because the husk and cob offer some natural protection, though whole-cob storage takes up considerably more space than shelled kernel storage.

Storage duration and pest-damage risk both depend heavily on grain moisture at the time of storage (properly dried grain resists insect and mould damage far better), the type of storage container (clean, sealable containers reduce insect entry and re-infestation), and ongoing pest monitoring. For longer-term storage (several months or more), some farmers use airtight containers or drums. A safe storage moisture target of roughly 14-15% is referenced in this source (consistent with the moisture level some farmers target at harvest for direct storage -- see the harvest maturity indicators topic).
